question: to the Commission Piotr Müller (ECR) Subject:

The European Health Data Space (EHDS) framework currently in the pipeline aims to create an integrated system for exchanging medical information to support innovation and improve healthcare across the EU. At the same time, the organisation and delivery of health services remain the competence of Member States, which raises questions as to the impact of a centralised digital infrastructure on the autonomy of national healthcare systems, the competitiveness of European businesses and the security of strategic health data. There is also a risk of market concentration around the largest global tech players, in particular from countries that do not guarantee democratic standards and data protection equivalent to EU law. In view of this, I ask: 1.
What financial instruments and procedural simplifications does the Commission envisage to ensure that the costs of certifying EHDS systems do not become a barrier for Polish and European SMEs?

What legal and technical mechanisms will be put in place to prevent entities from countries that do not meet democratic and data protection standards equivalent to EU law from using EU citizens’ health data?
Is the Commission monitoring the impact of digitalising health on the exclusion of older people and the risk of increased costs for health services as a result of market concentration?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (28.7.2026) The European Health Data Space (EHDS)1 Regulation establishes provisions for strengthening the single market of electronic health record (EHR) systems, reducing costs and barriers to entry. By harmonising rules for EHR systems, the compliance costs get lower for new entrants, including small and medium-sized enterprises. For example, the Regulation lays down a self-certification procedure for EHR systems limiting certification costs and administrative burdens for EHR systems manufacturers of all sizes, including small and medium-sized enterprises. Regarding use EU citizens’ health data by entities from third countries, the EHDS Regulation sets out a mechanism2 of reciprocal access that will serve to assess the rules in third countries to ensure that only entities from third countries recognised as providing similar rules will be able to apply for access. Transfers of personal data to third countries can only take place subject to the conditions and limitations set out in Chapter V of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR)3, notably the need to ensure a level of protection in the third country that is essentially equivalent to the one guaranteed within the EU4. When it comes to risks of digital exclusion among older populations, the EHDS promotes inclusive design usable for all, including older adults, enabling them to exercise their rights under the Regulation.
1 Regulation (EU) 2025/327 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 11 February 2025 on the

European Health Data Space and amending Directive 2011/24/EU and Regulation (EU) 2024/2847, OJ L, 2025/327, 5.3.2025, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2025/327/oj. 2 See Articles 75(5) and 91 EHDS Regulation. 3 Regulation (EU) 2016/679 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 April 2016 on the protection of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data and on the free movement of such data, and repealing Directive 95/46/EC (General Data Protection Regulation), OJ L 119, 4.5.2016, p. 1–88. 4 See also recitals 35 and 81 EHDS Regulation.
